title: The Broken Spar: the Abbé, the Integrant Molecule, and the Geometry of the Mineral Kingdom
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, birth in a weaver's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia agree on 28 February 1743 at Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, Oise. Coordinate taken from the commune's own fr.wikipedia point, 49 30 24 N / 2 25 54 E.
stops.campa: In the Picard town of Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, on the flat road between Paris and Amiens, a son is born to a family of weavers and named René Just Haüy. The loom is the household's trade and the parish is its horizon. A second son, Valentin, follows three years later and will invent the teaching of the blind; the town will one day raise a single monument to the pair of them. Nothing in the house suggests that the elder boy will spend his life breaking stones open to find the shape sitting inside them.
suggested_refs: The site of the Haüy family house at Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, now marked by a stele

stops.name: Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, the parish font
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: no reachable source names the baptismal church or the day. The date here is a placed day-after-birth, not a source date, and the present Church of Saint-Just is a nineteenth-century building.
stops.campa: The child is carried to the font of the parish he was born in. The building that stands in Saint-Just today under the name of Saint-Just went up in the following century, long after the family had gone, so the roof he was baptized under is not the roof a visitor sees. This is the first gap in his record. A priest's life begins in a parish whose baptismal register nobody quotes, in a town that remembers him chiefly through the brother who came after him.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of Saint-Just-en-Chaussée for 1743, not consulted in this research
sources: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Just-en-Chaussée (gap: no source names the baptismal church)

stops.name: Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, the Premonstratensian tonsure
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1762 and the Premonstratensian connection (fr.wikipedia); the place is [R], since no source names the house or abbey where the tonsure was conferred. Day and month unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At nineteen he is tonsured, taking the first formal step toward the priesthood among the Premonstratensians, the white canons whose houses stand thick across Picardy. The order teaches and preaches, and the vocation it opens for him is a schoolmaster's rather than a contemplative's. Within two years he will be in Paris standing in front of a class of boys. The Church that cuts his hair this year keeps its claim on him through the Revolution, through a prison cell, and into a canon's stall at Notre-Dame under Napoleon.
suggested_refs: The Premonstratensian houses of the Beauvaisis and the Oise, candidates for the unnamed site of the tonsure

segments.name: The Latin Quarter: Orders and Regencies

stops.name: Collège de Navarre, regent of the fourth class
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1764 (en.wikipedia); some chronologies place the teaching post before the minor orders and some after, and no source settles the sequence. Day and month unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He is appointed regent of the fourth class at the Collège de Navarre, on the slope of the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, and begins teaching grammar to boys of twelve. The stipend is small and the hours are long. The Latin Quarter becomes his entire country from this year: for the next fifty-eight he will teach, cleave crystals, be arrested, be decorated and die inside half a mile of these streets, and will never once leave France. The college buildings do not outlast the Revolution.
suggested_refs: The site of the Collège de Navarre on the rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève, later absorbed by the École Polytechnique

stops.name: Paris, the grades of the Church
stops.date_confidence: attested by year in en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia, which agree: minor orders 1765, subdeacon 1767, deacon 1769. No day, month or officiating church is given in either. This stop carries the three years; dated to the first.
stops.campa: He receives minor orders in the diocese of Paris, is ordained subdeacon two years later and deacon two years after that, climbing the grades of the Church at the same steady rate as he climbs the classes of the college. No source names the church where any of the three ceremonies is held. The Church pays him, lodges him and hands him the leisure a weaver's son would otherwise never see; the celibacy it asks in exchange leaves him at the end with no heirs but a brother and eight thousand stones.
suggested_refs: The ordination registers of the diocese of Paris for 1765, 1767 and 1769, not consulted in this research

stops.name: Paris, ordained priest
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1770 by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia, which agree; no day, month or church is given. Defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At twenty-seven he is ordained priest. He will never hold a cure of souls and never preach from a parish pulpit. He stays in the schools. His is the priesthood of a teaching abbé, one of thousands who staff the colleges of Paris in the last generation before the Revolution. Twenty-two years from this ordination it will put him in a prison cell with the September Massacres closing in, and thirty-two years from it the same ordination will make him, by Napoleon's order, a canon of Notre-Dame.
suggested_refs: The status of the abbés régents in the Paris colleges on the eve of 1789

stops.name: Collège du Cardinal-Lemoine, the Abbé Lhomond and the herbarium
stops.date_confidence: attested that the regency follows the 1770 ordination (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia, universalis); no separate precise date is given, so the year is taken from the ordination. Lhomond is listed among the college's professeurs célèbres.
stops.campa: He moves to the Collège du Cardinal-Lemoine on the rue Saint-Victor as regent of the second class. Among the masters there is the Abbé Charles Lhomond, grammarian and botanist, who takes him out walking to look at plants. Haüy learns the Linnaean system on foot and builds a herbarium, and the Academy will elect him a botanist on the strength of it. The rue Saint-Victor will matter again: at its far end, sixteen years from now, his brother Valentin starts teaching blind children to read.
suggested_refs: The site of the Collège du Cardinal-Lemoine, demolished after 1790, now crossed by the rue du Cardinal-Lemoine

stops.name: Jardin du Roi, the lecture of Daubenton
stops.date_confidence: [R] undated: en.wikipedia records the Daubenton lecture as the turning point without a year, and the geographic record places it during the Cardinal-Lemoine years, before 1783. 1780 here is a placed midpoint, not a source date.
stops.campa: Across the gardens of the Jardin du Roi, Louis-Jean-Marie Daubenton lectures on mineralogy to whoever will come in off the street, and the botanizing abbé comes. Daubenton shows crystals as bodies with fixed forms and constant angles. Haüy walks out of that hall a mineralogist and stays one for forty years. He never forgets who turned him: when he publishes his theory he prints his thanks to Daubenton in the preliminary discourse, beside Bézout and Laplace, who taught him the geometry that made his stones speak.
stops.quote: J'ai trouvé, si j'ose ainsi parler, une récompense bien précieuse de cette résolution dans les encouragemens que j'ai reçus de M. Daubenton.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784), Discours préliminaire, pp. 37-38 in the archive.org OCR of the Wellcome scan b28762411_0002; long-s modernized, 18th-century spelling 'encouragemens' kept. The research pool cited pp. 38-39; the page is unverified against printed pagination.
suggested_refs: Daubenton's public mineralogy courses at the Jardin du Roi in the 1770s

stops.name: Paris, the calcite breaks
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left open: fr.wikipedia dates the observation to 1781, en.wikipedia to 1783 or later. Dated here to 1781. The owner of the cabinet is given as Jacques de France de Croisset in some accounts and as 'the citizen Defrance' in Haüy's own 1801 retelling.
stops.campa: In a private cabinet in Paris a hexagonal prism of calcareous spar comes apart in his hands. The break is not a shatter: the crystal opens along a clean oblique plane with the shine of something polished by nature rather than by a lapidary. He carries it home and goes on cutting, plane after plane, until what is left is a small rhomb that will not divide into anything but rhombs of itself. Every account of the beginning of crystallography starts in this room, with this stone.
stops.quote: J'avois remarqué qu'un crystal de cette variété, qui s'étoit détaché par hazard d'un groupe, se trouvoit cassé obliquement, de manière que la fracture présentoit une coupe nette, & qui avoit ce brillant auquel on reconnoît le poli de la Nature.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784), Discours préliminaire, p. 10; archive.org OCR of b28762411_0002, long-s modernized, 1784 verb endings kept. Haüy says the crystal had detached from a group and broken, not that he dropped it.
suggested_refs: The mineral cabinet of Jacques de France de Croisset (Defrance), Paris

stops.name: The Louvre, elected to the Académie royale des sciences
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives 12 February 1783 and the rank of adjoint botaniste; fr.wikipedia gives the year and calls him associé-botaniste. The Académie royale des sciences sat in the Louvre, which fixes the coordinate.
stops.campa: The Académie royale des sciences, sitting in the Louvre, elects him adjoint botaniste. He is forty, a college regent with no degree in the sciences and no patron at court, and the seat comes to him for the work on crystals rather than for the herbarium his title names. The election is decided by vote among men who have spent their lives at mathematics. From this year the abbé of the fourth class has a hearing at the top of French science, and he uses it to read papers on garnet, on fluorspar, on spar.
stops.quote: Une observation que je fis sur le spath calcaire en prisme à six pans, terminé par deux faces exagones, me suggéra l'idée fondamentale de toute la théorie dont il s'agit.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784), p. 10; archive.org b28762411_0002. Written the year after the election, looking back at the observation the Academy had heard him report.
suggested_refs: The registers of the Académie royale des sciences for 1783, listing Haüy's memoirs on garnet and calcareous spar

stops.name: Paris, the Essai of 1784
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1784 by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia, which agree; no month is given. Defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux appears in Paris, one volume with folding plates. Its argument is that a crystal is a stack. Split any crystal of a given species along the planes it offers, and you arrive at one solid that repeats without end: the primitive form. All the varieties of outward shape that mineralogists had been cataloguing as separate kinds turn out to be the same brick laid in different courses. The mineral kingdom, until this book a museum of appearances, acquires a geometry.
stops.quote: De réduire, en un mot, la Cristallographie à une Science qui ait des principes fixes, d'où l'on puisse tirer des conséquences propres à répandre du jour sur une matière jusqu'ici enveloppée de tant d'obscurités.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784), p. 5; archive.org b28762411_0002. Orthography as presented in the research pool, modernized from the 1784 printing.
suggested_refs: The Wellcome copy of the 1784 Essai, digitized at archive.org as b28762411_0002

stops.name: Paris, the constituent molecules and the law of decrements
stops.date_confidence: attested: both doctrines are stated in the 1784 Essai. The pyramid of dates is firm; the page numbers in the research pool are not, two independent reads of the OCR placing the decrements passage at pp. 64 and 66.
stops.campa: The bricks themselves he calls molécules constituantes, later molécules intégrantes: particles that hung suspended in a fluid, drew one another in, and settled into polyhedra of regular figure. To get from the stack to the visible crystal he proposes the law of decrements. Each successive layer of molecules is laid short by one row, or two, or three, and the staircase of tiny steps reads to the eye as a single smooth face standing at a fixed angle. Small whole numbers govern the mineral kingdom, and he can compute them.
stops.quote: J'entends par molécules constituantes celles qui, suspendues d'abord dans le fluide où elles étaient en dissolution, se sont attirées mutuellement, et réunies pour former, par leur aggrégation, des polyèdres de figure régulière.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784), p. 49 in the archive.org OCR of b28762411_0002 (the research pool cited p. 50); orthography modernized, and the 1784 printing has '&' where this reads 'et'.
suggested_refs: The plates of the 1784 Essai, showing stepped stacks of cubes resolving into rhombic dodecahedra

stops.name: Paris, the electricity of crystals
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia: the calamine pyroelectricity work in 1785, the Exposition raisonnée in 1787. This stop carries both; dated to the earlier. Days and months are not given.
stops.campa: He heats calamine and finds that it takes a charge at its two ends, one pole positive and one negative, then does the same with tourmaline, the stone jewellers had long known would pull ash off a warm hearth. The charge does not belong to the substance alone: it follows the shape, appearing at the ends that the crystal's own geometry makes unequal. In 1787 he publishes the Exposition raisonnée de la théorie de l'électricité et du magnétisme. The man who counts rows of molecules is now measuring what the rows do.
suggested_refs: Haüy, Exposition raisonnée de la théorie de l'électricité et du magnétisme (Paris, 1787)

stops.name: Rue Saint-Victor, the other brother's raised letters
stops.date_confidence: attested in the corpus journey for Louis Braille: Valentin Haüy's Essai sur l'éducation des aveugles is dated 1786 and the Institution Royale des Jeunes Aveugles is his foundation. The fraternal link between Valentin and René Just is external biographical fact, not stated in that file [R].
stops.campa: On the rue Saint-Victor, a few doors from the college where his brother teaches Latin, Valentin Haüy is schooling blind children and printing books whose letters stand up off the page so that fingers can read them. His Essai sur l'éducation des aveugles appears this year. Thirty-three years later a boy from Coupvray named Louis Braille will arrive at this institution, read Valentin's embossed letters, find them slow, and replace them with dots. Two sons of a Picard weaver are teaching France to read surfaces by touch.
suggested_refs: Valentin Haüy, Essai sur l'éducation des aveugles (Paris, 1786), printed in raised type

stops.name: The Louvre, associate in natural history and mineralogy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1788 (en.wikipedia); no day or month given. Coordinate is the Louvre, seat of the Académie royale des sciences.
stops.campa: The Academy moves him out of botany and into natural history and mineralogy, the class where his work has been sitting all along. He is forty-five, and for one more year the institutions holding up his life stand where they have stood for a century: the Academy in the Louvre, the colleges on the mountain, the Church that ordained him. He goes on cleaving. Every specimen that reaches his table is cut in every direction it will accept, until the nucleus inside it lies bare in the light.
stops.quote: J'essayai si je ne pourrais point faire, dans ce même prisme, des coupes dirigées selon d'autres sens.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784), p. 10; archive.org b28762411_0002. Orthography as presented in the research pool, modernized from the 1784 printing.
suggested_refs: The classes of the Académie royale des sciences before 1793 and Haüy's transfer between them

stops.name: Paris, arrested as a prêtre réfractaire
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives 10 August 1792, tying the arrest to the fall of the Tuileries; fr.wikipedia gives August 1792 without a day. The prison is named in neither source, an open gap, and the coordinate is a generic Paris point.
stops.campa: The Tuileries falls, the monarchy goes down with it, and the hunt for priests who refused the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy begins in earnest. Haüy has refused it. He is taken and held in a Paris prison whose name no source gives. He is forty-nine years old, an academician of nine years' standing, and the Republic that will shortly ask him to define its units of measure has him locked up for a signature he would not put on paper. In the cells around him are men who will be dead in three weeks.
suggested_refs: The Paris prisons holding refractory clergy in August 1792 (Saint-Firmin, the Carmes, the Abbaye), none of them named by the sources for Haüy

stops.name: Paris, a student fetches him out
stops.date_confidence: [R] traditional: fr.wikipedia names Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, his student, as the intervener and places the release before the September Massacres; en.wikipedia corroborates the timing without naming anyone; the en.wikipedia article on Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire does not narrate the rescue at all. Day unknown.
stops.campa: Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, a naturalist of twenty and Haüy's own pupil, goes to the prison with other men of the Jardin des Plantes and has his teacher let out. Within days the mobs enter the prisons of Paris and kill more than a thousand of those still inside. The priest who would not swear walks away alive because a student came for him. Geoffroy will sail to Egypt with Bonaparte, hold a chair at the Muséum, and spend thirty years quarrelling with Cuvier about the unity of the animal plan.
suggested_refs: The September Massacres of 2-6 September 1792 and the release of academicians beforehand

stops.name: Paris, weighing water with Lavoisier
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia dates the joint task of determining the density of water to 4 January 1793. The meeting place is not specified; the coordinate is a generic Paris point.
stops.campa: The Republic wants a unit of mass fixed by nature rather than by a king's forearm, and hands the job to two men: Antoine Lavoisier, who has taken chemistry apart and reassembled it by weight, and the abbé Haüy. Their task is the density of distilled water, because the new kilogram is to be a cubic decimetre of it. Lavoisier is the same academician who nine years earlier sat on the royal commission that examined Franz Mesmer's animal magnetism and reported that no such fluid existed. The two weigh water all winter.
suggested_refs: The 1793 determination of the density of water underlying the definition of the kilogram

stops.name: The Louvre, the Academy abolished and the commission named
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Convention dissolved the academies on 8 August 1793 (en.wikipedia); Haüy was appointed to the Temporary Commission of Weights and Measures on 11 September 1793 (en.wikipedia; fr.wikipedia gives the year alone). This stop carries both, dated to the first.
stops.campa: On the eighth of August the Convention abolishes the academies of the old regime, and the Académie royale des sciences, a hundred and twenty-seven years in the Louvre, stops existing by decree. Five weeks later the same Convention names twelve men to the Temporary Commission of Weights and Measures, and Haüy is one of the twelve, and takes the secretaryship. The body that elected him is gone. The work continues in a room with no letterhead, fixing the metre and the kilogram for a country that is guillotining its own chemists.
suggested_refs: The decree of 8 August 1793 suppressing the academies; the Commission temporaire des poids et mesures

stops.name: Place de la Révolution, Lavoisier beheaded
stops.date_confidence: attested: 8 May 1794. The place is the Place de la Révolution, today the Place de la Concorde, which en.wikipedia names as the site of Lavoisier's execution; the research pool's coordinate lay 1.5 km east and is corrected here.
stops.campa: On the eighth of May, on the Place de la Révolution, Antoine Lavoisier goes to the guillotine with twenty-seven other farmers-general, tried and condemned inside a single afternoon. The Republic that is measuring the meridian in order to build its units of mass has just cut the head off the man who was weighing the water. Haüy stays on as secretary of the commission. He keeps the minutes, he keeps his own head, and the kilogram when it is finally fixed rests on a density Lavoisier did not live to publish.
suggested_refs: The Place de la Concorde, formerly Place de la Révolution, site of Lavoisier's execution

segments.name: Year III: the Metre and the Institute

stops.name: Hôtel des Monnaies, the Cabinet of Mineralogy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the decree of 12 July 1794 reorganizing the École des Mines and ordering a Cabinet of Mineralogy (en.wikipedia). Contradiction left open on the curatorship: en.wikipedia dates it to October 1794, fr.wikipedia dates his conservatorship and chair of crystallography to 1795. The first lectures on the law of symmetry are [R], placed in 1795.
stops.campa: A public decree of the twelfth of July reorganizes the École des Mines and orders a Cabinet of Mineralogy for it. The school is lodged in the Hôtel des Monnaies on the Quai de Conti, and the collection is put into Haüy's hands: first curator, first professor of crystallography, and the man who lays out the drawers. The specimens are arranged by his own classification, species by primitive form. Here he first teaches the law of symmetry, that whatever a crystal does to one face it does to every face of that kind.
stops.quote: les décroissements se feront par des soustractions d'une simple rangée de molécules d'une figure exactement cubique.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784); archive.org b28762411_0002, page cite unreliable, two OCR reads placing it at pp. 64 and 66 against the pool's p. 65. The sentence belongs to a worked example on the rhombic dodecahedron, not to a general statement of the law.
suggested_refs: The Musée de Minéralogie of Mines Paris, whose founding collection Haüy arranged

stops.name: Amphitheatre of the Muséum, the École normale de l'an III
stops.date_confidence: attested: Haüy was appointed professor of physics on 9 November 1794 (en.wikipedia), but fr.wikipedia gives the school's actual run as 1 pluviôse an III (20 January 1795) to 30 floréal an III (19 May 1795). Dated here to the opening. The school is not the later École normale supérieure.
stops.campa: On the first of pluviôse, year III, the Republic opens a school to manufacture teachers for the whole nation and crams some fifteen hundred students, sent up from every department, into an amphitheatre of the Muséum. Haüy is professor of physics. Stenographers take down every lecture for printing, so that departments too poor to send a man can read what Paris heard. The school lasts four months and closes on the thirtieth of floréal. It is the largest audience the abbé will ever stand in front of.
stops.quote: Cette forme, indiquée par la Nature même, ainsi qu'on le verra bientôt, et non pas prise arbitrairement et comme au hasard, est dans le sel marin celle d'un cube parfait.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784), p. 49; archive.org b28762411_0002. Orthography as presented in the research pool, modernized from the 1784 printing.
suggested_refs: The printed Séances des Écoles normales de l'an III, stenographic record of the four-month school

stops.name: Paris, the metric system made law
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia dates the formal establishment of the metric system in France to 7 April 1795, the law of 18 germinal an III.
stops.campa: The law of 18 germinal, year III, gives France the metric system with its names: metre, gram, litre, are, and the decimal ladder tying them together. The metre is a ten-millionth of the quarter meridian; the gram is the mass of a cubic centimetre of water at its densest. Haüy's part is in the second of those, the weighing that began with Lavoisier two winters before and continued after Lavoisier's head came off. A weaver's son from Picardy has helped fix the units most of the world will measure by.
suggested_refs: The law of 18 germinal an III establishing the metric system

stops.name: The Louvre, the Institut National
stops.date_confidence: attested: 22 August 1795, corroborated independently at fr.wikipedia's article on the Académie des sciences. fr.wikipedia places Haüy's entry into the Institut in 1795 without a day. The Institut was first installed in the Louvre.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of August the Convention creates the Institut National des Sciences et des Arts, and the abolished Academy walks back into the Louvre under a new name. Haüy is in the class of physical and mathematical sciences from the start. Three years later Bonaparte, a member of the same class, founds an Institut d'Égypte at Cairo explicitly on this model. The Republic has discovered that it cannot do without the institution it destroyed, and the mineralogist has outlived both versions of it.
suggested_refs: The founding classes of the Institut National des Sciences et des Arts, 1795

stops.name: Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, the mineralogy chair
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left open: fr.wikipedia dates his Muséum teaching from 1800, en.wikipedia his professorship to 1802. Daubenton died 31 December 1799 and his successor Dolomieu was imprisoned in Italy until March 1801 and dead by November 1801, which would let both dates stand for different things, but no source says so. Dated to 1800.
stops.campa: Daubenton, who turned him toward minerals twenty years before, dies on the last day of 1799. His successor in the Muséum chair, Déodat de Dolomieu, is in an Italian prison and will be dead within a year of getting out of it. Haüy takes up the teaching of mineralogy at the Jardin des Plantes in the gap and is confirmed in the chair once Dolomieu is gone. He lectures from specimens, cleaving while he talks, taking off the outer matter cut by parallel cut until the nucleus inside stands exposed on the bench.
stops.quote: en sorte qu'en enlevant par des coupes successives et parallèles toute la matière appliquée sur ce noyau, on pouvait aisément le mettre à découvert.
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Essai d'une théorie sur la structure des crystaux (Paris, 1784), p. 52; archive.org b28762411_0002. Orthography as presented in the research pool, modernized from the 1784 printing.
suggested_refs: The chair of mineralogy at the Muséum, held by Daubenton, then Dolomieu, then Haüy

stops.name: Paris, the Traité de minéralogie
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1801. The apparent contradiction over volume count is not one: the standard collation is four text volumes plus a separately bound atlas, counted as four by en.wikipedia and five by fr.wikipedia, whose 1801-1823 span covers the atlas and later issues rather than serial publication.
stops.campa: The Traité de minéralogie appears in Paris: four volumes of text with a bound atlas of plates, printed at the Republic's expense. Every mineral species is defined by its primitive form and by the decrements that generate its varieties, and the engravings show the stacks brick by brick. Abraham Gottlob Werner at Freiberg, where Alexander von Humboldt learned his mineralogy in under a year, classifies instead by external character and origin. The two systems split European mineralogy, and Haüy's is the one that lasts.
stops.quote: The observation I have just noted is that which has served to develop my ideas on the structure of crystals. It presented itself in the case of a crystal that the citizen Defrance was kind enough to give me just after it had broken off from a group...
stops.quote_source: Haüy, Traité de minéralogie (Paris, 1801), quoted in English translation on en.wikipedia, 'René Just Haüy'. Not verified against the original French; the wording is Wikipedia's translation and should be treated with caution.
suggested_refs: The atlas volume of the Traité de minéralogie, 1801

stops.name: Notre-Dame de Paris, honorary canon
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives 5 April 1802; fr.wikipedia gives the year without a day.
stops.campa: Napoleon, First Consul, having just signed the Concordat and reopened the churches, makes the mineralogist an honorary canon of Notre-Dame de Paris. The refractory priest of 1792, arrested for refusing an oath, is installed in the cathedral chapter by the same state that arrested him. He keeps the stall and the stipend that goes with it. He is a canon of Notre-Dame and a member of the Institut National des Sciences et des Arts in the same year, and he gives up neither.
suggested_refs: The chapter of Notre-Dame de Paris reconstituted under the Concordat of 1801

stops.name: Quai de Conti, the Institut under the dome
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1805 (fr.wikipedia, Institut de France); no day or month given. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the corpus pin for the Institut de France in the Gustave Eiffel journey, which that file flags as a placeholder for the building.
stops.campa: By Napoleon's order the Institut leaves the Louvre and crosses the river into the Collège des Quatre-Nations, Mazarin's domed foundation on the Quai de Conti, a few hundred paces from the Hôtel des Monnaies where Haüy keeps his crystals. He sits under that dome for the rest of his life. The building will still be handing out honours a century afterwards, when Gustave Eiffel is decorated there in his eighties for work on wind resistance. It is where France keeps the names it intends to keep.
suggested_refs: The Collège des Quatre-Nations, 23 Quai de Conti, seat of the Institut de France from 1805

stops.name: Lake Nemi, a blue stone takes his name
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1807 and for the namer, Tønnes Christian Bruun-Neergaard (en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia). Type locality is Lake Nemi in the Alban Hills, Rome province (en.wikipedia, Haüyne); the research pool's placement near Vesuvius and its Rome city coordinate are both errors, corrected here.
stops.campa: In the Alban Hills south of Rome, in the volcanic rock around Lake Nemi, a deep blue glassy mineral is found, and the Danish mineralogist Tønnes Christian Bruun-Neergaard names it haüyne for the abbé in Paris. Haüy has never left France and will never see the locality. The species carries the name of a man who did not describe it, found in a country he does not visit. The name will outlast every title and salary he holds. Napoleon's canon becomes a blue stone.
suggested_refs: Haüyne from the type locality at Lake Nemi, Alban Hills, Latium

stops.name: The Sorbonne, a chair made for one man
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1809 (fr.wikipedia), consistent with the creation of the imperial faculties; no day or month. Coordinate is the Sorbonne, seat of the Faculté des Sciences.
stops.campa: The imperial university is built, and a chair of mineralogy is created at the Faculté des Sciences of Paris for Haüy alone. He is sixty-six and holds, at one time, the Muséum professorship, the Cabinet at the École des Mines, his seat under the dome on the Quai de Conti, the canonry of Notre-Dame and the Légion d'Honneur. Napoleon has made his textbook required in the schools. The weaver's son is the most decorated scientist in France, and every post he holds is held at the emperor's pleasure.
suggested_refs: The chair of mineralogy at the Faculté des Sciences de Paris, created 1809

stops.name: Paris, stripped by the Restoration
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the 1911 Britannica states only that 'after 1814 he was deprived of his appointments by the government of the Restoration. His latter days were consequently clouded by poverty.' No source enumerates which posts were lost, and he appears to have kept the Muséum chair and lodging until his death. Anchored to the first Restoration, 1814.
stops.campa: The emperor abdicates, the Bourbons come back, and the government of the Restoration takes away what its predecessor gave. Haüy is seventy-one. The salaries stop and the pension goes unpaid, and the man who helped fix the units of the Republic and taught the empire its mineralogy ends his life poor, lodged at the Muséum with his blind-school brother. He goes on cleaving specimens for the second edition of the Traité, which he will finish and not long survive.
suggested_refs: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Haüy, René Just', on the poverty of his last years

stops.name: Paris, the Hundred Days and the law of symmetry
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1815 on both counts (en.wikipedia): promotion to officer of the Légion d'Honneur during the Hundred Days, and the full publication of the law of symmetry. Neither is given a day. He had received the order itself on 28 November 1803.
stops.campa: Napoleon comes back from Elba for a hundred days, and inside that window Haüy is promoted officer of the Légion d'Honneur, twelve years after first receiving the order. In the same year the law of symmetry, which he has been teaching from the bench since 1795, is finally published in full: the faces of a crystal repeat according to the symmetry of the form underneath, and the repetition can be counted. Waterloo comes in June. The promotion is signed by a government that has stopped existing.
suggested_refs: Haüy's law of symmetry as published in 1815 and restated in the Traité de cristallographie

stops.name: New York, the Lyceum of Natural History
stops.date_confidence: [R]: en.wikipedia's Haüy article gives an 1817 honorary membership of what it calls the New York Academy of Sciences. The name is anachronistic: the body was founded on 29 January 1817 as the Lyceum of Natural History, and its own article does not list Haüy, so the membership rests on the Haüy article alone.
stops.campa: In New York, at the end of January, a handful of physicians and naturalists found the Lyceum of Natural History, the society that will later rename itself the New York Academy of Sciences. Haüy is made an honorary member of it. He is seventy-four, stripped of his French salaries, and being elected by a republic across an ocean that has read his Traité and has a continent of unclassified minerals to put in order. The system travels better than the man, who has still never crossed a French border.
suggested_refs: The founding minutes of the Lyceum of Natural History, New York, 29 January 1817

stops.name: Paris, the Traité de cristallographie
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1822, two volumes plus atlas. Not a second edition of a book of that title: the Traité de cristallographie is the recast second edition of the Traité de minéralogie under a new name, and no first edition bears the crystallography title. No month given.
stops.campa: The Traité de cristallographie appears, two volumes and an atlas: the Traité de minéralogie rebuilt and renamed for the science rather than for the kingdom of objects it describes. Crystallography now has a discipline's title page. He is seventy-nine and has been at the same question for forty-one years, since a prism of spar came apart in his hands in a stranger's cabinet. The book is published in the last months of his life, and the discipline it names is still his when X-rays confirm the stacks ninety years on.
suggested_refs: Haüy, Traité de cristallographie (Paris, 1822), 2 vols with atlas

stops.name: Muséum lodgings, the death of Valentin
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia's article on Valentin Haüy dates his death to 19 March 1822 and places the brothers in a shared lodging at the Muséum.
stops.campa: Valentin Haüy dies in the lodging at the Muséum that the two brothers have shared for years, infirm and by then not going out at all. He had taught the first blind children in France to read raised letters, taken his pupils to perform before the king at Versailles, and been pushed out of his own school. Three years before this, a boy from Coupvray named Louis Braille entered that school and read the books Valentin had printed. René Just outlives his brother by two months and a fortnight, in the same rooms.
suggested_refs: The brothers' shared apartment at the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle

stops.name: Paris, the fall and the wrong date
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1 June 1822: en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia converge on it and both flag 3 June as a commonly repeated error, corrected by Alfred Lacroix in 1944. The 1911 Britannica still prints 3 June; fr.wikipedia gives 3 June as the burial date. The exact address near the Muséum is not given.
stops.campa: A fall in his room breaks his femur and he never gets up from it. He dies on the first of June, seventy-nine years old, in the quarter he has lived in since he was twenty-one. Georges Cuvier, writing the Academy's eulogy the following year, gives the date as the third of June, and that error stands in the reference books for a hundred and twenty-one years until the mineralogist Alfred Lacroix corrects it in 1944. The founder of crystallography spends over a century carrying the wrong day.
suggested_refs: Cuvier's 1823 eulogy of Haüy, and Alfred Lacroix's 1944 correction of the death date

stops.name: Père-Lachaise, division 60, his brother's grave
stops.date_confidence: attested: burial on 3 June 1822 at Père-Lachaise, division 60, chemin Gosselin, in the same grave as his brother (fr.wikipedia; appl-lachaise.net). The Barbier de la Serre grave in division 53 is attested in the corpus journey for Barbier.
stops.campa: He is buried on the third of June at Père-Lachaise, division 60 on the chemin Gosselin, in his brother's grave. The stone names Valentin. For a hundred and seventy years the founder of crystallography lies in Paris under somebody else's name, seven divisions from the plot where Charles Barbier de la Serre, the artillery officer whose night writing gave Louis Braille his dots, is buried under a plaque that names the Association Valentin Haüy. The surname does the remembering; the mineralogist waits.
suggested_refs: The Haüy brothers' grave, Père-Lachaise division 60, chemin Gosselin

segments.name: The Afterlife of the Integrant Molecule

stops.name: Berlin, Weiss lectures and Fröbel listens
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the corpus journey for Fröbel dates his arrival at Christian Samuel Weiss's Berlin crystallography lectures to 15 October 1812 and calls Weiss 'the great crystallographer'. The descent of Weiss's classification from Haüy's theory is external history, not stated in that file.
stops.campa: In Berlin, Christian Samuel Weiss lectures on crystal form to a student from Thuringia named Friedrich Fröbel, and builds his own classification of mineral forms straight out of the Frenchman's theory. Fröbel becomes Weiss's assistant at the royal mineralogical museum, ordering specimens by their fixed geometries, and takes away a conviction he never lets go of: that form is law, and that children should be handed it early. The Gifts he later gives to kindergarten children are a sphere, a cylinder and a cube.
suggested_refs: Christian Samuel Weiss's crystallographic system and its debt to Haüy; Fröbel's Gifts

stops.name: École des Mines, the portrait and the bust
stops.date_confidence: attested: portrait by Nicolas Gosse, 1843, and bust by Lisbeth Delisle, 1993 (fr.wikipedia). This stop carries both, dated to the earlier. The school moved to the boulevard Saint-Michel under the ordinance of 6 December 1816, after Haüy's time at the Hôtel des Monnaies.
stops.campa: At the École des Mines, moved by now up to the boulevard Saint-Michel, Nicolas Gosse paints his portrait in 1843, and Lisbeth Delisle makes a bust of him in 1993, a century and a half apart, for a school of mining engineers that has never stopped teaching out of the collection he arranged. Satyendra Nath Bose comes to Paris in the 1920s to learn X-ray crystallography under Alexandre Dauvillier, reading with rays the stacked lattices this abbé had inferred with a knife and a good eye.
suggested_refs: The Musée de Minéralogie, Mines Paris, boulevard Saint-Michel

stops.name: Stowe House, the collection sold and bought back
stops.date_confidence: attested: heirs sold the collection to the Duke of Buckingham in 1823 over the Muséum's counteroffer, and Armand Dufrénoy repurchased it for the Muséum at the 1848 Stowe auction (fr.wikipedia); en.wikipedia's Stowe House article records the 1848 dispersal after the second duke's bankruptcy. Dated to the repurchase. The research pool's coordinate lay 7 km off and is corrected.
stops.campa: Haüy's heirs sell the collection in 1823, over eight thousand specimens together with the wooden models he cut to demonstrate the decrements, to the Duke of Buckingham, turning down a counteroffer from the Muséum. The crystals cross to Stowe in Buckinghamshire. Twenty-five years later the second duke goes bankrupt and Stowe is emptied at auction, and the mineralogist Armand Dufrénoy buys the collection back for the Muséum. The founder's own stones cross the Channel twice in a generation.
suggested_refs: The 1848 Stowe House sale; the Haüy collection in the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle

stops.name: Galerie de minéralogie, seated opposite Cuvier
stops.date_confidence: attested: the seated statue by Isidore Hippolyte Brion is dated 1863 and stands in the central nave of the Galerie de minéralogie et de géologie, facing a statue of Cuvier (fr.wikipedia). Coordinate is the gallery's own point; the research pool's lay 280 m northeast.
stops.campa: In the gallery of mineralogy and geology at the Jardin des Plantes, Isidore Hippolyte Brion sets a seated Haüy in the central nave, facing a seated Cuvier: the man who classified the mineral kingdom placed opposite the man who classified the animal one and got his death date wrong. Around the two statues the collection is still ordered on his principle, species by primitive form. Elsewhere in the same garden a medallion of him is set into the façade of the evolution gallery, and a covered walk carries his name.
stops.quote: Happening to let fall a specimen of calcareous spar belonging to a friend, he was led by examination of the fragments to make experiments which resulted in the statement of the geometrical law of crystallization associated with his name.
stops.quote_source: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Haüy, René Just', via Wikisource, retrieved as an automated summary rather than a verified verbatim excerpt [R]. This is the popular dropped-crystal version, which conflicts with Haüy's own 1784 and 1801 accounts of a crystal that had detached from a group and broken.
suggested_refs: Brion's 1863 seated statue of Haüy, Galerie de minéralogie et de géologie, Paris

stops.name: The Eiffel Tower, thirteenth on the southeast face
stops.date_confidence: attested that Haüy stands thirteenth on the southeast face among the seventy-two names (en.wikipedia); dated here to the tower's inauguration year, when the names were inscribed. No day given.
stops.campa: Gustave Eiffel has the names of seventy-two French scientists cut in letters two feet high around the first balcony of his tower. HAÜY stands thirteenth on the southeast face. He is up there in gold with Lavoisier, who was beheaded on the Place de la Révolution, and with Fourier and Poisson and Dulong, over a city where a weaver's son taught grammar to twelve-year-olds for a small stipend, refused an oath, weighed water for the Republic, and never once left the country whose units he helped to fix.
suggested_refs: The seventy-two names on the Eiffel Tower, southeast face

stops.name: Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, the brothers in bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1903 sculptural group before the town hall and for the eclogite stele on the site of the family house (fr.wikipedia); no day given. The street in Saint-Just, the rue Just Haüy at Amiens and the Amiens faculty amphitheatre are attested without dates.
stops.campa: Saint-Just-en-Chaussée puts up a sculptural group in front of its town hall: Valentin teaching a blind child, René Just among his minerals, the weaver's two sons in bronze in the square they were born beside. On the site of the family house a stele is set of eclogite, the metamorphic rock René Just was first to describe, in the Traité of 1822, so that the stone marking the birthplace is a species he named. Amiens gives him a street in the Noyon suburb and an amphitheatre at its faculty of sciences.
suggested_refs: The 1903 monument to the Haüy brothers before the town hall of Saint-Just-en-Chaussée

stops.name: Père-Lachaise, both names at last
stops.date_confidence: [R]: fr.wikipedia dates the marble plaque to the 1990s without a year and credits the municipality of Saint-Just-en-Chaussée with donating it. Anchored here to 1990-01-01 as a decade placeholder.
stops.campa: At Père-Lachaise a marble plaque is added to the brothers' grave, paid for by the municipality of Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, and for the first time both names stand on the stone: the savant minéralogiste and the premier instituteur des aveugles. It has taken a hundred and seventy years and the initiative of a Picard town of six thousand people. The crystallographer's grave is finally legible, which is the thing his brother spent an entire working life arranging for other people.
suggested_refs: The 1990s plaque on the Haüy grave, donated by Saint-Just-en-Chaussée
